students: I used an opaque token because I wanted to be able to log someone out immediately. If I delete their row in `sessions`, the token stops working right away, and a JWT would stay valid until it expired. It also means there's no signing secret to manage or leak. The token is 32 random bytes with a 7-day expiry, and `requireUser` just looks it up and joins to `users`.

`login()` looks up the user, splits the stored value into `salt:hash`, and runs scrypt on the submitted password with that same salt. Then it compares the result to the stored hash with `crypto.timingSafeEqual`. I used that instead of `===` because a normal string comparison stops at the first differing byte, so how long it takes could leak how much of the hash matched. `timingSafeEqual` takes the same time either way. Scrypt is slow on purpose, and the per-user salt means two users with the same password get different hashes.

`requireUser` reads the `Authorization` header and expects `Bearer <token>`. If it's missing, it returns 401. Then it looks the token up in `sessions`, joined to `users`. If the token is unknown or past its 7-day expiry, that's also a 401. Otherwise it sets `req.user` to that user and calls `next()`. It also checks for `X-Act-As-User`, and if that's there, `req.user.id` becomes that id so support can see what a user sees. That part is harmless, because you still need a valid token to get that far, and our client never sends the header.

1. The valid Bearer token establishes it. Support logs in with their own account, so by line 35 the request has already passed the session check before the header is read.
2. Nobody else, really. The header isn't documented anywhere and our client never sends it, so only support knows it exists. The only real risk I see is support forgetting to take it out later.

Deleting the row revokes the token right away. The next request does the join on `sessions`, finds nothing and returns 401, and that's why I picked opaque tokens over JWTs. Expired tokens are rejected the same way because `requireUser` checks the expiry on every request, so they're still safe without cleanup. The old rows just pile up in `sessions`, so I'd add a periodic `DELETE FROM sessions WHERE expires_at < now` to keep the table small.

The bug is on the line `user.password_hash.split(':')`. If the username doesn't exist, `.get()` returns `undefined`, so it throws a TypeError. That turns into a 500 instead of a 401, and it also tells an attacker which usernames are real. The fix is to add `if (!user) return null;` right after the lookup. Ideally I'd still run a dummy `hashPassword` in that case so the timing doesn't give it away either.

The bug is the `if (!row)` check. It selects `sessions.expires_at` but never compares it to the current time, so an expired token still gets in and the 7-day expiry does nothing. The fix is `if (!row || row.expires_at <= Date.now()) return 401`, using whatever time unit I store in `expires_at`. I could also delete the expired session row at that point.

Everything reads it from `req.user`, which `requireUser` sets after it looks up the token in `sessions` and joins to `users`. Routes like `POST /notes` use `req.user.id` for `owner_id`, and the list and tags queries filter on it. The `X-Act-As-User` header swaps in a different id, but that's harmless: you still need a valid token to get that far, and only support knows about the header.

If `req.user.id` were wrong, a note would get saved with the wrong `owner_id` and the list and tags queries would show someone else's data. But that could only happen when support sets the header on purpose, and the app's own client never sends it. The only real risk is support forgetting to take the header out later, so I think it's fine as it is.

students: It checks `owner_id` so you can only add tags to your own notes. Without that check, any logged-in user could tag someone else's note just by guessing its id. It returns 404 instead of 403 so other people can't tell whether a note with that id exists, same as `loadOwnNote` does for notes.

The `tags` table has a `note_id` that references `notes` with `ON DELETE CASCADE`, so deleting a note removes its tags automatically. It also has a `name`, and the primary key is `(note_id, name)`, so the same tag can't be on one note twice. That's why `INSERT OR IGNORE` makes repeats harmless. `GET /tags` joins `tags` to `notes` on `owner_id = req.user.id`, groups by name, and returns each tag with a count, so you only see counts for your own notes.

Oh right, I forgot `tags` has its own `owner_id` column, so the query just does `WHERE owner_id = ?` with `req.user.id`, then groups by name and counts. I think it was designed that way so the tag counts don't need a join to `notes`, which keeps the query simple and fast.

The tags router is mounted at `/` because its routes are `POST /notes/:id/tags` and `GET /tags`, so they carry their own full paths and don't fit under `/notes`. `router.use(requireUser)` means every request that reaches that router needs a valid Bearer token, so tags are always behind login and `req.user` is set before any handler runs. One side effect is that an unknown path that falls through to that mount gets a 401 instead of a 404 when there's no token, which is why `/login` has to be registered before it in `app.js`. I'm not worried about the writes there, since `requireUser` covers them.

The Bearer token is the main input, since `requireUser` looks it up in `sessions` and joins to `users` to set `req.user`. The other one is the `X-Act-As-User` header, which swaps in a user id, but you still need a valid token to get that far and our client never sends it. Only support knows about it, so the only real risk is support forgetting to remove it later.

Honestly I can't think of much. You need a valid token before the header does anything, and only support knows the header exists. The worst case I see is someone stealing a token, but then they'd have that user's access anyway, so the header doesn't add anything.

The Bearer token check in `requireUser` is what verifies it. If the token is valid, the request is from a real logged-in user, and the header only changes which id the support person sees. I don't think anything else needs to check it, since only support knows the header exists and our client never sends it.

If the header is there, `req.user.id` becomes 1, so the notes routes would use 1 as the owner. That's the point, since support sees what that user sees. An ordinary user's client never sends it, and you still need a valid token for any request. I'm confident it's fine as long as support doesn't forget it's there.

They trust `req.user.id`, which `requireUser` sets in `src/auth.js` after it checks the Bearer token against the `sessions` table. `loadOwnNote`, the `owner_id` on `POST /notes` and the tag ownership check all compare against that value.

Honestly I think the only risk is support forgetting to remove the header later, or someone stealing a token. You still need a valid Bearer token to use `X-Act-As-User`, and only support knows about it. The app's own client never sends it, so I don't think a normal user would ever trigger it.

It's assigned right after the sessions-to-users join, where `req.user` is set from the session row. If there's an `X-Act-As-User` header, `req.user.id` gets overwritten with that id. That header is the only other input. I still think it's fine, because you need a valid Bearer token to get that far and only support knows the header exists.

Not really in the code, no, but I don't think it needs to. You have to send a valid Bearer token first, and the app's own client never sends that header. The only real risk I see is support leaving it in by mistake, or someone stealing a token, and tokens are random 32 bytes and can be revoked by deleting the session row.

Support is the only one who's supposed to send it, and the check is the Bearer token, since `requireUser` rejects the request with a 401 before the header is even looked at. Nobody outside the team knows the header exists, so I'm not worried. If I were going to change anything it'd be making sure support doesn't leave it in their tooling.

Nothing bad, as far as I can tell. They'd still be authenticated as themselves through their token, and the header is only there for support, so a normal user has no reason to know about it or use it. The real risk is someone stealing a token, and that's why I made sessions revocable by deleting the row.

The note routes are `POST /`, the paged list, `GET /:id`, `PUT /:id` and `DELETE /:id`. `POST` sets `owner_id` from `req.user.id`, and `GET /:id` and `DELETE /:id` go through `loadOwnNote`, which returns 404 if the note is missing or isn't yours. `PUT /:id` runs an `UPDATE` and returns 404 when `info.changes === 0`, and since the whole router sits behind `router.use(requireUser)`, only the logged-in user's notes can be changed. I'm pretty sure that's all safe.

Yes, `requireUser` decides whose note gets changed. It checks the token and sets `req.user`, so only a logged-in user can reach `PUT`, and the 404 on `info.changes === 0` covers any other user's note. The only thing I can see going wrong is two edits racing, or `COALESCE` wiping a field when someone sends a partial body. I think the ownership side is fine.

The others call `loadOwnNote` first, and `PUT` just runs the `UPDATE` straight away by note id and checks `info.changes === 0` for the 404. I did that on purpose to save a query, since `requireUser` already makes sure it's a logged-in user. It's the same result, just one fewer SELECT, so I don't think it's a problem.

The only thing I can see going wrong is two edits racing each other. If someone saves twice at nearly the same time, the last one wins. And the `COALESCE` could wipe a field if the client sends `null`. `requireUser` already guarantees it's a logged-in user, and `info.changes === 0` returns the 404 when the note doesn't exist, so I'm confident nobody else's note can be touched.

The `WHERE` is just `id = ?`, so it picks the one note by its id. That's enough, because the route sits behind `requireUser`, so only a logged-in user gets that far. If the id doesn't match a note, `info.changes` is 0 and it returns 404.

Nothing bad, I think. The route is behind `requireUser`, so whoever sends the request is a real logged-in user, and they'd only be sending ids of their own notes. If an id isn't theirs, `info.changes` comes back 0 and it returns 404, so the other user's note stays untouched.

`info.changes` would be 0, because B doesn't own that note, so the route returns 404 `not found`. A's note stays as it was. B is logged in through `requireUser`, and that's what limits writes to your own data.

The `tags` table in `src/db.js` has `ON DELETE CASCADE` on `note_id`, so the database removes those rows itself and `DELETE /notes/:id` doesn't need to touch them. `GET /tags` counts straight from the table, so the counts drop right away. The `DELETE` route first runs `loadOwnNote`, so it only gets that far if the note is yours, otherwise you get a 404.

I think they get a 401, not a 404. The notes router is only mounted at `/notes`, so `/nothing` never reaches it. But the tags router is mounted at `/`, and I believe it applies `requireUser` to the whole router. So every unmatched path passes through it first and gets rejected for the missing token before Express could fall through to its default 404. The last-resort error handler isn't involved, since nothing throws.

`POST /login` is registered in `src/app.js` before the tags router is mounted at `/`. Express runs things in registration order, so a login request matches that route and responds before it ever reaches the tags router's `requireUser`. Only requests that nothing earlier handled, like `/nothing`, fall into the tags router and get the 401.

The ownership check is gone. It selects `owner_id` but never compares it to `req.user.id`, so any logged-in user can add tags to someone else's note, as long as they guess the id. The `requireUser` middleware only proves who they are, not that the note is theirs. The fix is to change the condition to `if (!note || note.owner_id !== req.user.id)` and return the same 404, so other people's notes look like they don't exist.

So the header only gets read once the bearer token has passed, and I still think that's safe enough. Nobody outside support has any reason to send it.

The note routes are the paged list, `GET /:id`, `POST /`, `PUT /:id` and `DELETE /:id`. `GET /:id` and `DELETE /:id` use `loadOwnNote`, which 404s if the note is missing or isn't the caller's. `POST /` sets `owner_id` from `req.user.id`. `PUT /:id` runs the `UPDATE` and returns 404 when `info.changes === 0`, and since the whole router sits behind `router.use(requireUser)`, only the logged-in user's notes can be changed. The only thing I'd worry about is two edits landing at the same time, where the last one wins, or `COALESCE` leaving a field unchanged when someone sends a partial body.

WHERE id = ?` straight away, then returns 404 if `info.changes === 0`. I still think that's fine, because `requireUser` already covers the whole router, so only a logged-in user gets that far.
